title: Day 5: Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Your degree plan helps you prepare for graduation. During your time at BYU, you can also hear new ideas, meet people who are doing work that interests you, and try things that help you find your direction. You do not have to pursue every opportunity. This lecture offers ways to find and evaluate a few that matter to you.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Review from last week

What did your Day 4 graduation plan help you see?

Think about one course or sequence you want to investigate.
Then ask a partner: What would you still want to know about the experience of studying data science at BYU?

Start here. Give students one minute to recall Day 4’s comparison of majors, prerequisites and first graduation-plan draft. Allow another minute to talk. Invite answers about people, research, experiences, questions, workload and life on campus. The plan contains the courses but cannot tell the whole story. About 3 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: The plan shows part of your education
text:
The plan shows part of your education
Your courses build important foundations in computing, statistics, mathematics, and applications.

What can you learn alongside those courses?


Continue directly from the review. Day 4 covered catalog requirements, MyMAP, the MAP sheet and advising, so do not repeat the catalog walkthrough. Show this as an expansion of what a BYU education can include, not a criticism of required coursework. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Day 5: Building Your BYU Experience
What can you gain from opportunities beyond your required courses?

This is the title slide, placed after the review as requested. The throughline: college offers access to people and opportunities while you focus on developing yourself. You cannot do everything. You can learn to notice, ask, try and reflect. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
You have room to explore
College gives you a period focused on learning, with access to people who study and work on questions you may never have encountered.

Some opportunities will change how you think about your direction.

You have other demands on your time. Finding a few worthwhile experiences matters more than doing everything.

Do not imply that all students have abundant free time. Many work, have family responsibilities or commute. The useful distinction is having nearby opportunities and people during a season devoted in part to learning. Keep the tone invitational, not a productivity lecture. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: Even within Data Science, there is a lot to discover
text:
Even within Data Science, there is a lot to discover



Methods


Statistics, machine learning, computing, mathematical models, visualization




Questions and settings


Health, sports, science, public policy, business, the arts, and more




Being sure of your major does not mean you already know which parts of the field you will enjoy.


Address the student who has already chosen Data Science. Exploration can happen within a single degree. Avoid asking students to rank their strengths before they have experienced these areas. Ask for one question they are curious about, even if it is tentative. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: What a course may not show you
text:
What a course may not show you
An event or experience can introduce you to:

a question you had not considered
people working on that question
a way of doing the work that you might enjoy or want to change


Give a concrete example: a student goes to a research talk about a field they do not know and leaves with a question for the speaker, even though much of the technical content goes over their head. Attending once can be worthwhile. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Ways to begin



An hour or an afternoon


Forum, research talk, guest speaker, club meeting, student poster session




A longer commitment


Club project, research group, internship, student leadership



Start with a visit or a conversation. You can decide later whether to do more.

Explain that a first visit is a useful experiment. A student can attend a club meeting or hear a talk without committing to an ongoing project. Experiences differ in cost of time and in what they reveal. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
People you can talk with

A TA about how they approached a course, or what helped when they got stuck
An advisor about courses, a possible change in direction, or an experience you want to fit into your plans
A professor about something from class, their research, or an idea you want to explore

You can go to office hours simply because you are curious.

Day 4 introduced the advisement center. These are examples of things students might discuss, not prescribed scripts or limits on what these people can help with. Connect briefly to the existing advisor and TA lab assignment. Faculty office hours also welcome students with curiosity or incomplete ideas. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Ask what it was like

An older student may know which events they would attend again, what surprised them about research, or how they found an internship.

Ask people about their experience. Then decide what sounds worth trying for yourself.

Being social can be hard. A useful conversation can begin with one sincere question. Do not frame social ease as a prerequisite for belonging or career success. Other people’s experiences can help students spend their limited time well. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: What could a club give you?
text:
What could a club give you?



Ideas and practice


Hear what students are making, learn a tool, or work alongside them.




People and perspective


Ask an older student how they chose courses, projects, research, or internships.




You can go to one meeting to see what it is like.


Introduce these possibilities before telling the club story. If a club representative is present, invite a brief description of what a newcomer could do at the next event. Avoid overpromising that every club offers every benefit. Link to BYU’s official associations page in the reference slides. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: My experience in the Data Science club
text:
My experience in the Data Science club

How did being involved change what I learned or who I met?



What I expected. What I actually found. What I would tell a student who is new to a club.



Personal story prompt for Dr. Kerby. Supply your actual undergraduate Data Science club experience orally. Do not invent dates, offices held, projects or outcomes. Include a human detail about the first meeting and a tangible benefit that did not come from coursework. About 3 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Research starts with curiosity
You might begin by reading a faculty member’s description of their work or attending a talk.

“I am interested in this question. How could an undergraduate learn more about the work?”

You can ask what preparation would help, even if there is no current opening.

Demonstrate finding one faculty description on the BYU Data Science faculty page if useful. A good inquiry names a specific interest and asks how to learn more. Do not promise a position or urge students to send generic messages to every professor. Research can involve many subjects and departments. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
My search for research work

How did I look for a research assistant position?



Where I looked. Whom I approached. What I learned from the search itself.



Personal story prompt. Tell the actual RA search, including uncertainty or a request that went nowhere if relevant. Students benefit from hearing the steps, not only the eventual outcome. Research positions and qualifications vary across groups. About 3 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Informational interviews: a reminder
Ask someone about their work and what they have learned.

“What skill matters in your work that job descriptions often leave out? How could a student develop it?”

If advice is useful, try it. Tell the person what happened afterward.

Recall Day 3: the purpose is learning about a person and their work, not asking for a job. Students can follow up with an update when they act on good advice, which can begin an informal mentoring relationship. One thoughtful question is enough to get started. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: An informational interview changed my direction
text:
An informational interview changed my direction
After returning from my mission, I had an informational interview at Myriad Genetics.
That conversation helped me decide to study statistics.

What did I learn that I might not have learned from a degree description?


Tell your own story here. The stated facts come from Dr. Kerby: an informational interview at Myriad Genetics after his mission influenced his decision to study statistics. Fill in what was actually said and how it changed your thinking. Do not invent the professional’s role or their advice. This reinforces Day 3’s informational interview assignment. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: A second conversation can change your plans
text:
A second conversation can change your plans
I felt prompted to attend a BYU graduate fair.
That experience helped steer me toward Data Science, rather than statistical genetics.

Tell your graduate-fair story as you experienced it, including your account of feeling the Spirit prompt you to go. Students may understand the experience in different ways. Keep the focus on being willing to attend and talk with people, even when your direction seems settled. Do not supply additional career chronology or details that Dr. Kerby has not provided. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: A first question can be small
text:
A first question can be small



To an older student


“What was worth attending when you first got here?”


“What would you try again?”




To a faculty member


“What led you to this research question?”


“How could I learn more?”




Normalize that starting a conversation can feel awkward. Faculty office hours and club gatherings provide built-in reasons to talk. Invite students to adapt these prompts rather than recite them. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Internships: where to start looking

Read what employers actually ask people to do.
Watch BYU Handshake and career opportunities and the AI & Data Science newsletter.
Ask older students and faculty how they found work they enjoyed.
Build evidence of useful work through courses, projects, or research.


About 3 minutes. Practical guidance, not a claim that everyone needs an internship immediately. Demonstrate how a posting reveals skills to develop, as students practiced on Day 3. Tell students that experience may be called research, an internship, a campus job, or a project; evaluate the work itself. BYU’s career page links to Handshake and BYU Connect. Source: https://datascience.byu.edu/career-opportunities and https://datascience.byu.edu/newsletter.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Which opportunities deserve your time?
There is more to try than you can fit into a semester.
Read the description. Ask someone who went. Try one that interests you.
An older student’s view can help you judge what you might learn from an event. Your own experience can change that judgment.

Avoid ranking experiences by prestige. The learning payoff differs by person and moment. Some events are social, some technical, some an introduction to a new question. Free food can get someone through the door, but ask what else the experience might offer. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Five past BYU events
Which one would you have been curious to attend?

The five examples occurred in 2025 or 2026 and are past as of October 12, 2026. They are for discussion, not an announcement that students can attend them now. We found an original flyer for the research conference and documented descriptions for the other events. One account of the club case competition comes from a student participant. Give groups time to compare initial reactions. About 30 seconds.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: A flyer and a campus fair
text:
A flyer and a campus fair


 View the original research conference flyer

Student Research ConferenceMarch 8, 2025. Students presented research across the college.




AI & Data Science Launch Event and Fair


Club representatives, professors, advisors, demos, games, and food.


September 25, 2025


What might you do there besides eat?




Past events: BYU Chemistry flyer and BYU Data Science fair listing.


Show the actual public flyer if BYU’s image host allows it to load; an official source link remains available if it does not. The research conference flyer describes the March 2025 conference. The 2025 fair is documented on BYU Data Science’s past events page and explicitly included club representatives and free food. Ask who might enjoy either and what someone could ask when they get there. About 1 minute. Sources: https://www.chem.byu.edu/news/call-for-student-research/ and https://datascience.byu.edu/past-events.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
A workshop and a forum



Family History Technology Workshop


Talks on handwriting recognition, data modeling, machine learning, and other technology.


March 2, 2026




Francis S. Collins BYU forum


“The Road To Wisdom: On Truth, Science, Faith and Trust.”


January 27, 2026




Past events: workshop and BYU Speeches forum archive.


Historical examples. The forum broadens exploration beyond a direct technical or career payoff. The workshop demonstrates how data science appears in another domain. Do not imply that a first-year student could necessarily register for every past event: this is an evaluation exercise about interest and value, not a current opportunity listing. Sources: https://fhtw.byu.edu/ and https://speeches.byu.edu/talks/?event_type=forum. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
A Statistics Club event
BYU Statistics Club case competition
In 2026, students worked on a data problem and shared what they found. One participant presented maps of New York City rat complaints.

Would you rather attend an event like this, join a team, or talk with someone who took part?


Student participant’s account · BYU Statistics Club


We could not verify a flyer for an ASA kickoff. This is a real club activity in 2026 documented in a participant’s account. BYU lists the Statistics Club as its ASA student chapter. Do not imply that this event is currently open for registration or that this one student’s experience represents everyone. The different levels of engagement, from watching to joining a team, make it useful for discussion. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Your first impression
Choose one of the five events you would have considered attending.

What caught your interest? What might you hope to learn or experience there?

Write your answer privately, then compare with a partner.

Think for 40 seconds, talk for a minute. Invite students to choose any of the five. Do not ask them to justify why they would skip the others. A student may value the forum for understanding relationships between science and faith even if it will not help with a resume. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: What an event listing cannot tell you
text:
What an event listing cannot tell you

What would you ask a student who has attended something like it?

Possible questions:

What did people actually do there?
Could someone new to the subject follow along?
What did you get out of going?


Collect one question per pair and take a few aloud. Speaking with older students can reveal what it was like to attend or participate. The slides do not invent reviews of these events. About 2 minutes.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Discuss the tradeoffs
In small groups, compare two events.

What might you gain from each? What could make either less worthwhile for you right now?

Would an older student’s experience change your initial choice?

About 3 minutes. Keep discussion grounded in the descriptions, not fabricated reports about event quality. Possible tradeoffs: a campus fair offers breadth and people but can feel crowded; a research conference exposes specific questions but technical detail may be hard to follow; a workshop connects data to a domain but may require more background; a club competition offers practice but takes more time; a forum may broaden perspective without an immediate technical payoff. These are possibilities, not verified reviews. Invite multiple views.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: Time spent can have several kinds of value
text:
Time spent can have several kinds of value
You learn something. A new question stays with you.
You meet someone. A conversation opens another door.
You discover a preference. You learn what you want more of, or less of.

Debrief the event activity. Disliking a session can still clarify a preference, provided students approach the event with curiosity. These are possible benefits, not guaranteed outcomes of attendance. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
section: Where to find the next one
text:
Where to find the next one


AI & Data Science newsletter for events, jobs, and internships


Student associations for meetings and projects


Faculty directory for research questions and people


College advisement for help with your plan



Show these as live links or direct students to the home page. The newsletter aggregates BYU events and opportunities, while specific clubs and faculty pages may change. Encourage students to check current listings before attending. About 2 minutes. Sources: each linked official BYU page.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Your next conversation
Name one person or group you could ask about an opportunity that interests you.

What would you want to know from them?

An advisor, professor, TA, club member, older student, or professional could each help answer a different question.

This is a reflection, not an additional graded networking requirement. Link it to the advisor and TA lab assignment and Day 3’s professional exploration. Give 30 seconds to write and take one or two volunteers. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
You cannot do it all

You can choose a few things to try while you have access to them.

The next event or conversation does not have to settle your future. It can help you decide what to explore next.

Keep the invitation proportionate to students’ constraints. This closes the lecture’s main argument and makes the next slide an easy attendance exit ticket. About 1 minute.

title: DS 115 | Building Your BYU Experience
text:
Exit ticket

What is one kind of opportunity at BYU you had overlooked?
Why might it be worthwhile for you?
What is one question you could ask someone who knows more about it?


Use these questions for the daily attendance quiz if appropriate. Answers can be tentative and need not disclose private plans. Allow about 2 minutes. End the active lecture here. The next slides are references.
